# Varsity by Zfolio: Modern Portfolio Theory - Risk Parity & HRP

**Duration:** 12 minutes | **Level:** Intermediate

## The Question Markowitz Doesn't Quite Answer

The **Efficient Frontier** lesson showed you the curve of best possible portfolios, and flagged its central practical weakness: classic Mean-Variance Optimization needs to invert a covariance matrix to find a point on that curve, and with real stock data, that matrix is often close to singular (nearly un-invertible), especially when holdings are few or highly correlated (see the **Correlation Matrix** lesson for why real assets rarely move fully independently). The result: tiny estimation errors in your inputs can produce wildly different "optimal" weights. A change of a few basis points in one stock's estimated volatility can flip the recommended allocation from 40% to 4%. This is not a theoretical nitpick — it's the single biggest reason textbook mean-variance optimization is rarely used unmodified in practice, and it's the exact gap this lesson picks up.

**Risk parity** sidesteps the problem entirely by asking a different question: instead of "what mix maximizes return for a given risk" (which requires forecasting returns, the hardest and least reliable input of the three MVO needs), it asks **"what mix means every holding contributes the *same amount of risk* to the portfolio?"** No return forecast, no matrix inversion required — just each asset's own volatility.

> 📊 **Figure:** an illustrative side-by-side allocation, ₹1 lakh split five ways — equal-rupee weighting next to risk-parity weighting, showing capital shift away from a volatile small-cap and toward a bond ETF — is pictured just below.

## Why "Equal Rupees" Isn't "Equal Risk"

Most first-time investors build a portfolio by splitting money evenly — ₹10,000 each into five stocks. That's equal **capital** weighting. It is very rarely equal **risk** weighting, because different stocks carry very different volatility.

**Illustrative example:**

| Holding | Capital | Annual Volatility | Risk Contributed |
|---|---|---|---|
| HDFC Bank (large-cap) | ₹10,000 (20%) | 18% | Low |
| ITC (large-cap, defensive) | ₹10,000 (20%) | 15% | Low |
| Govt Bond ETF | ₹10,000 (20%) | 4% | Very low |
| A volatile small-cap | ₹10,000 (20%) | 45% | High |
| Gold ETF | ₹10,000 (20%) | 13% | Low-medium |

Even though every row has the same rupee amount, the small-cap position is doing most of the *work* — its 45% volatility means it swings the portfolio's day-to-day value far more than the bond ETF's 4% ever will. An "equal weight" portfolio is quietly a concentrated bet on whichever holding is most volatile.

**Simple risk parity** (also called "inverse volatility weighting") rebalances this: it gives *less capital* to the volatile small-cap and *more capital* to the bond ETF, until each position's contribution to total portfolio risk is roughly equal. The portfolio ends up more bond- and gold-heavy in rupee terms than an equal-weight split would suggest — not because bonds are "better," but because a rupee of small-cap and a rupee of government bond are not the same amount of risk.

But simple risk parity has its own blind spot, and it's the same one MVO struggles with from a different angle: it only looks at each asset's *own* volatility in isolation. It has no concept of correlation at all. Two large-cap IT stocks with +0.85 correlation (see the **Correlation Matrix** lesson) get treated as two fully independent risk sources, when in reality they're close to the same bet placed twice. This is the gap Hierarchical Risk Parity was built to close.

## Three Distinct Approaches, Side by Side

Before going further, it's worth being precise about the fact that there are genuinely **three different algorithms** in play across this module, not two:

| Approach | What it optimizes for | Needs return forecasts? | Needs matrix inversion? | Accounts for correlation structure? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mean-Variance Optimization (MVO)** | Maximum return for a given risk | Yes | Yes (unstable on real data) | Yes, but fragile to estimation error |
| **Naive / Equal-Weight "Risk Parity"** | Equal risk contribution per asset, using only each asset's own volatility | No | No | No — treats every pair as independent |
| **Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP)** | Equal risk contribution, allocated through a correlation-aware cluster structure | No | No | Yes — explicitly, by design |

HRP is not "risk parity with extra steps," and it is not "MVO but safer" — it is a genuinely distinct algorithm that borrows the *goal* of risk parity (balance risk contribution, not capital) while borrowing the *awareness of correlation structure* that made MVO powerful in theory, without inheriting MVO's matrix-inversion fragility. Getting this distinction right matters, because the three methods can produce meaningfully different portfolios from the exact same holdings.

## Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP): The Actual Mechanism

**Hierarchical Risk Parity**, introduced by Marcos López de Prado in [a 2016 paper](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2708678), works conceptually in three stages. It's worth understanding each one at the level of *what problem it solves*, not just as a checklist:

**1. Cluster assets by correlation, building a hierarchy.** Using the correlation matrix from the previous lesson, HRP measures how "close" every pair of holdings is — highly correlated pairs (like two large-cap IT stocks) are treated as "near" each other, while low-correlation pairs (like a stock and a gold ETF) are treated as "far apart." It then builds these pairwise distances up into a **hierarchical tree**, sometimes visualized as a **dendrogram** — first grouping the most similar assets into small clusters, then grouping those clusters into larger ones, all the way up to a single tree containing every holding. The result looks less like a flat list of assets and more like a family tree: TCS and Infosys might branch together early (they're similar), that IT branch might later join a broader "Indian equities" branch, which eventually joins the full portfolio tree alongside a separate "defensive assets" branch containing gold and debt.

**2. Reorder holdings so the structure is visible.** The raw correlation matrix, before clustering, is essentially a random-looking grid — similar assets can sit anywhere in it. HRP reorders the rows and columns so that assets grouped together by the tree in step 1 sit physically next to each other in the matrix. This step doesn't change any numbers, only their arrangement — but it turns a noisy grid into something with visible block structure, clusters of high correlation sitting together, that the next step can actually use.

**3. Allocate risk top-down through the tree, splitting at each branch.** Instead of solving for all weights simultaneously (which is where matrix inversion and its instability come from), HRP starts at the top of the tree and works down: at each branch point, it splits the risk budget between the two child branches in inverse proportion to each branch's own combined variance — the calmer branch gets more of the budget, the more volatile branch gets less. It then recurses into each branch and repeats the split, all the way down until every individual holding has a weight. A cluster of five highly correlated IT stocks, because they collectively count as roughly "one" volatile branch during this top-down split, ends up sharing a risk budget that a single, uncorrelated stock might get on its own — which is exactly the correlation-blindness problem that naive risk parity had, now fixed.

The payoff of this extra structure: **HRP never inverts the covariance matrix at any step.** It only ever compares two branches to each other at a time, splitting a budget between them — an operation that stays numerically well-behaved even with noisy, real-world data, unlike inverting a large matrix that's nearly singular. Because it works top-down through clusters instead of solving everything at once, small estimation errors in individual correlations don't cascade into wild swings in the final weights the way they can with mean-variance optimization. This directly answers the fragility the **Efficient Frontier** lesson raised about MVO: HRP was built, quite deliberately, as a response to that exact weakness — not a general-purpose improvement, but a targeted fix for "the covariance matrix is unstable and inverting it amplifies noise."

## Why This Approach Holds Up in Practice

Because it sidesteps matrix inversion entirely and doesn't require forecasting future returns, Hierarchical Risk Parity has become one of the more practical, real-world-tested approaches for building diversified allocations out of correlated holdings. It stays numerically well-behaved even with the kind of noisy, limited price history an individual investor's actual holdings realistically provide — which is exactly the situation a portfolio tool applying these ideas to your real holdings has to handle well. Tools that lean on correlation-aware, cluster-based allocation are drawing on the same three-stage idea covered above: cluster, reorder, then split the risk budget top-down through the tree.

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Risk Parity** | Allocating capital so every holding contributes roughly equal risk, not equal rupees |
| **Inverse Volatility Weighting** | The simplest, "naive" form of risk parity — weight inversely proportional to each asset's own volatility, ignoring correlation |
| **Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP)** | López de Prado's correlation-aware algorithm: clusters assets into a hierarchy by correlation, then allocates risk top-down through that tree, without inverting the covariance matrix |
| **Dendrogram** | A tree diagram showing how assets are grouped by correlation, from most similar pairs up to the whole portfolio |
| **Covariance Matrix Inversion** | The unstable step classic Markowitz optimization depends on and HRP deliberately avoids |

## Takeaway

✅ Equal rupee amounts are not equal risk — a volatile holding dominates portfolio risk even at the same capital weight as a stable one.
✅ Naive risk parity fixes the equal-capital problem using each asset's own volatility, but ignores correlation entirely — treating correlated assets as independent risk sources.
✅ Hierarchical Risk Parity is a genuinely distinct algorithm from both MVO and naive risk parity: it clusters assets into a hierarchy by correlation, then allocates risk top-down through that tree instead of inverting a covariance matrix.
✅ This design directly targets the exact weakness the Efficient Frontier lesson flagged in MVO — unstable, error-amplifying matrix inversion — which is why HRP holds up better on real, noisy market data.
✅ Because it needs no return forecasts and no matrix inversion, HRP is a practical, real-world-tested choice for correlation-aware portfolio tools working with limited, noisy holdings data.

**Next lesson:** "Understanding Risk Metrics" in the Risk Management module — now that you've seen how a correlation-aware method like HRP allocates risk, a closer look at how risk itself gets measured, including the CAGR, Sharpe, Sortino, and Calmar numbers used throughout this course.

quiz.question: Why doesn't naive (equal-weight) risk parity fully solve the problem that Hierarchical Risk Parity addresses?
options: Naive risk parity requires forecasting future returns, which HRP avoids
Naive risk parity only considers each asset's own volatility and ignores correlation between assets, treating correlated holdings as independent risk sources
Naive risk parity can only be used with fewer than five holdings
Naive risk parity always produces the same weights as classic MVO
quiz.explanation: Naive risk parity balances risk based only on each asset's individual volatility. It has no way to recognize that two highly correlated assets (like two IT stocks) are effectively similar bets, so it can understate how concentrated the portfolio's real risk is.

quiz.question: What is the core mechanism HRP uses to allocate risk, instead of inverting a covariance matrix?
options: It clusters assets into a hierarchy by correlation, then splits the risk budget top-down through that tree, branch by branch
It picks the single lowest-volatility asset and allocates all capital to it
It solves a system of linear equations across all assets simultaneously, just like MVO
It randomly assigns weights and iterates until returns are maximized
quiz.explanation: HRP builds a correlation-based hierarchy (often visualized as a dendrogram), then recursively splits the risk budget between branches in inverse proportion to their combined variance — never requiring the matrix inversion step that makes MVO unstable.

quiz.question: Why does avoiding covariance matrix inversion make HRP more robust than classic Mean-Variance Optimization on real, noisy market data?
options: Because matrix inversion is illegal to use in Indian financial products
Because inverting a near-singular matrix amplifies small estimation errors into large, unstable weight changes, while HRP's branch-by-branch splits stay numerically well-behaved
Because HRP doesn't use any correlation data at all, so there's nothing to be unstable
Because matrix inversion is only unstable when there are more than 100 assets
quiz.explanation: The Efficient Frontier lesson flagged that MVO's covariance matrix is often close to singular with real data, so inverting it can turn tiny input errors into wildly different 'optimal' weights. HRP sidesteps this entirely by never inverting the matrix — it only ever compares two branches at a time.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the three approaches: MVO, naive risk parity, and HRP?
options: They are all mathematically identical and just use different names

MVO maximizes return for given risk using forecasts and matrix inversion; naive risk parity balances risk using only individual volatility; HRP balances risk through a correlation-aware hierarchy without matrix inversion
HRP is simply naive risk parity run twice for extra accuracy
MVO and HRP both require return forecasts, but naive risk parity does not
quiz.explanation: Each method solves a genuinely different problem: MVO optimizes return-per-risk but needs fragile return forecasts and matrix inversion; naive risk parity balances risk but ignores correlation; HRP balances risk while accounting for correlation structure, without inverting the covariance matrix.

quiz.question: Why is Hierarchical Risk Parity considered a practical choice for real-world portfolio tools, compared to classic Mean-Variance Optimization?
options: It requires more precise return forecasts, which makes it more accurate
It needs no return forecasts and never inverts the covariance matrix, so it stays numerically stable on noisy, real holdings data
It ignores correlation entirely, which makes the calculation faster
It only works when a portfolio has fewer than five holdings
quiz.explanation: HRP's practical edge comes from what it doesn't need: no forecasted returns to get wrong, and no covariance matrix inversion to go unstable on noisy, real-world data — which is exactly the situation most real portfolios present.
